newsitem.title: INDIA: Infrastructure said holding up Indian growth plans.
newsitem.headline: Infrastructure said holding up Indian growth plans.

text.p: A slowdown in infrastructure growth threatens to hold back India's ambitious economic expansion plans, a senior Indian official said on Wednesday.
"The lack of infrastructure is catching up with the growing economy," R.H. Patil, managing director of the National Stock Exchange, told Reuters in an interview.
"The available infrastructure has been stretched to the limit after two years of good growth," Patil said.
"Hereafter, it will become more and more difficult to sustain a high rate of growth unless substantial investments are made in infrastructure," he said.
Patil's warning came a day after port delays forced India's leading refiner to cancel a diesel import tender, a move which analysts said highlighted India's infrastructure constraints.

Traders said the state-run Indian Oil Corporation cancelled the tender to import high-speed diesel because of port congestion. Earlier this year, it cancelled two tenders for kerosene imports for the same reason, they said.
Officials say India loses millions of dollars every year in demurrage payments because of the lack of port facilities.
Growth in the core sector -- power, roads and ports, for example -- is already showing signs of a slowdown which bodes ill for the long term, analysts said.
Industry Ministry figures released on Monday revealed a sharp growth slowdown from April to July 1996 in power, steel and petroleum sectors, compared with the same period last year.
Growth slipped to 2.1 percent in electricity from 12.4 percent and in steel to 5.3 percent from 11.7, the ministry said. Petroleum grew by 10 percent against 22.3 percent.

India's economy recorded year-on-year gross domestic product growth of seven percent in 1995/96 (April-March) and 6.3 percent in 1994/95 but is expected to post a growth of less than six percent in the current year, analysts said. The government has set a GDP growth target of 6.6 percent this year.
Analysts estimate that India needs investment of $200 billion over the next 10 years to develop the kind of infrastructure needed to sustain high economic growth.
Investments of this magnitude cannot be met through domestic sources, they say, and there is little evidence of foreign investor interest in Indian infrastructure projects.
"A break-up of FDI (foreign direct investment) actual inflows shows a concentration in the consumer goods and automobile sectors," James Capel B&K said in a recent report on the Indian economy.
At least 37 percent of FDI inflows have been in the consumer durables and automobile sectors while the services sector has attracted around 20 percent, the report said.
Investment in the capital goods sector is around 16 percent of total FDI inflows, it said.
"Given the current scenario, little improvement is likely in the immediate future in roads, railways and port sectors," according to Anindya Chatterjee, analyst at James Capel B&K.
"The government's plans to privatise ports is not taking off," he said. "Turnaround time in India is measured in days while the international norm is in hours."
Little improvement could be expected in the rail network with the Indian Railways having to resort increasingly to high-cost market borrowings to fund their projects, he added.
